title: Databricks & the Future of the Firm | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: Ben Horowitz argues Databricks (7B run rate, +80% y/y, agents now outnumbering humans in queries) is building a system of record for agents that lets firms automate information routing, flatten hierarchy, and own their learning loops. The thesis is a second managerial revolution where everyone becomes a manager of agents and competitive advantage lies in owning data and feedback loops rather than renting models.

insights.claim: Databricks has passed a $7 billion revenue run rate, growing 80% year over year, and was valued at $190 billion as of October 2026.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Benchmark for late-stage data/AI platform scale and valuation; growth at this size signals durable AI-data demand.
insights.locator: The Best Idea You'll Ever Have

insights.claim: Agents now generate more queries on Databricks than humans do, and agents launch more than 17 million databases per day, versus every interaction involving a human three years ago.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that machine users, not people, are becoming the main consumers of database infrastructure.

insights.claim: Lakebase, launched last year, has already crossed a $100 million revenue run rate with agents as its most prolific users, and Ghodsi thinks the agent-era database market may eventually exceed the existing database market.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Operational-database spend could shift to agent-oriented Postgres/lake architectures, a risk to incumbent database vendors.
insights.quote: We think that is probably going to be a bigger market in the long run than the existing database market

insights.claim: The Lakehouse business runs at more than $1.5 billion revenue run rate, growing over 100% year over year.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Shows the lakehouse architecture is a mainstream, fast-compounding category rather than a niche.

themes.theme: Architecture S-curves: Spark to Lakehouse to Lakebase

insights.claim: Databricks is framed as four stacked technology S-curves over nearly two decades (Spark, Lakehouse, Lakebase, agents), each creating the innovation window for the next, rather than a data company that merely caught the AI wave.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Durable platform moats come from compounding architectural unlocks, a pattern for judging infrastructure incumbents.
insights.quote: a data company that caught the AI wave

insights.claim: Hadoop's design of saving results to disk between rounds made it slow for iterative machine learning, and Spark's in-memory reuse of data while keeping fault tolerance made such workloads up to ten times faster.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Origin story shows how an architectural bottleneck fix created a company; look for analogous bottlenecks in agent workloads.

insights.claim: Spark was open source and free, so Databricks had to create value (easier, faster, more secure, enterprise-ready) faster than the free alternative could catch up; agents lowering switching costs will subject more companies to the same test.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Open-source-plus-managed-service economics and agent-lowered switching costs pressure software pricing power broadly.
insights.locator: Databricks built this muscle early on

insights.claim: Table-layer projects (Delta Lake, Hudi, Iceberg), developed independently by Databricks, Uber and Netflix, gave data lakes warehouse-like guarantees, which made the lakehouse merging lake and warehouse possible.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Open table formats are the enabling layer for unified data architecture; relevant to warehouse incumbents and format competition.

insights.claim: Lakebase applies the lakehouse idea to operational databases by separating storage from compute, so changes to transactional data are instantly available to analytics and agents without fragile pipelines; Databricks calls this unification LTAP.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Collapsing the OLTP/OLAP divide threatens ETL/pipeline vendors and standalone operational database players.

insights.claim: Because Lakebase copies only changes, even petabyte-scale databases can be duplicated in seconds, letting an agent branch a database, experiment, and discard it; Databricks says it did not fully appreciate this agent use case until recently.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Database branching like code is a native agent primitive that could shape database purchasing criteria.
insights.locator: This separation makes the database behave more like code

insights.claim: Databricks acquired Neon in 2025, a serverless Postgres company whose databases were already created mostly by AI agents, to form Lakebase.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: M&A signal: agent-generated database creation is already a real workload worth buying.

insights.claim: The shift is from a few databases managed by a central team and read by thousands of employees to thousands of databases that millions of agents read and write.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Database count and write volume scale with agents, a demand driver for serverless, cheap-storage architectures.
insights.locator: This technological unlock has come just in time

themes.theme: Agent capability and the context problem

insights.claim: Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi asserts AGI is already here, citing frontier models solving more than half of Humanity's Last Exam's 2,500 expert-written questions.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: A vendor CEO's framing; note the claim supports selling agent infrastructure, so discount for incentive.
insights.quote: We believe AGI is already here
insights.locator: A System of Record for Agents

insights.claim: METR data shows the length of task an agent can finish on its own has doubled roughly every seven months since 2019, and if it holds through the early 2030s agents could do tasks that take a human years.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: An exponential task-horizon trend underpins bullish agent-adoption timelines; monitor whether it keeps holding.

insights.claim: Since ChatGPT's 2022 launch, agent coding capability has moved from tasks taking a person about thirty seconds to tasks taking a skilled engineer a full work day.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Concrete measure of capability gain relevant to engineering labor demand.

insights.claim: The bottleneck for enterprise agents is context, not intelligence: most companies still do not trust AI to reliably update records in Salesforce.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Value accrues to whoever supplies governed company context and permissions, not only to model makers.
insights.quote: AI does not have an intelligence problem
insights.locator: A System of Record for Agents

insights.claim: A company's ontology (what exists, how it relates, what words mean, which source governs) is never finished and largely lives in experienced employees' heads, so agents can act autonomously only if ontology, authority and evaluation move into a system of record.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Frames a new enterprise software category, the system of record for agents, with Databricks contesting it against Palantir and SaaS vendors.

insights.claim: Databricks' Genie Ontology and its OntoRank algorithm (weighing author, usage breadth and recency) raised agent answer accuracy from about 50% to 84.5% when grounding agents in the company's ontology.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Vendor-reported evidence that grounding is the main lever for enterprise agent reliability.

insights.claim: Agent identity and access must change because per-employee logins break when employees spin up hundreds of agents a day; Unity Gateway gives each model and agent an identity, budget, guardrails and action traces.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Agent governance, identity and cost control is an emerging security/software spend category.
insights.quote: You can’t grant access to each proprietary, siloed database to your agents

insights.claim: Every enterprise platform shift produced a new fight over the system of record (IBM mainframe; Oracle and SAP client-server; Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow SaaS), and agents are the next shift.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Implies incumbent SaaS systems of record face disruption risk and an open contest for the agent-era record.
insights.locator: Every platform shift in enterprise computing

insights.claim: Palantir CEO Alex Karp argues all market value will go to chips and ontology, which the article says is rarely explained concretely.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: The ontology claim aligns Palantir and Databricks as competitors for the same enterprise layer.
insights.quote: All of the value in the market is going to go to chips and what we call ontology
insights.locator: A System of Record for Agents

themes.theme: Coase, Simon and the changing shape of the firm

insights.claim: Coase's logic is that firms expand until the cost of organizing a transaction internally equals buying it on the market; falling coordination costs from agents shift that boundary.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Gives a first-principles lens for forecasting firm size and outsourcing under AI.

insights.claim: Herbert Simon observed that centralizing a business's memory decentralizes its decisions, because a shared record lets decision points act independently and be reconciled automatically.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Explains why a shared agent record could push decision-making to the edges.

insights.claim: The database era did not make firms uniformly larger or smaller; it widened the range of firms that could exist, and AI is likely to raise the complexity ceiling of viable businesses and markets in the same way.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Expect both larger complex conglomerates and tiny capability-renting firms, not one direction.
insights.locator: Because both external and internal transaction costs fell

insights.claim: The twentieth-century pyramid firm used hierarchy as its information-processing system, and managers' choices over what to collect limited what the company could know about itself.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Information-routing middle layers are the part of management most exposed to automation.
insights.locator: The typical firm of the twentieth century

insights.claim: Knowing and doing barriers are falling together: natural-language interfaces let domain experts query and build without SQL or Python, as Novo Nordisk scientists query obesity data via Genie and a Rivian finance analyst with no SQL built a CFO revenue dashboard.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Customer proof points that non-engineers are producing internal software, reducing demand for intermediary data teams.
insights.quote: The hottest new programming language is English.

insights.claim: Jack Dorsey's Block is testing an extreme version in which a continuously updated world model coordinates work; Dorsey argues companies move fast or slow based on information flow and that hierarchy impedes it.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Block is a live public-company experiment in flattening management with AI; watch its efficiency metrics.
insights.quote: Companies move fast or slow based on information flow

insights.claim: Ghodsi differs with Dorsey: the org chart and information flow used to be the same thing but are no longer, so firms will keep managers for developing people and judgment but need fewer information routers.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Suggests middle-management compression rather than elimination.
insights.quote: Ten, twenty years ago, these were the same thing.

insights.claim: Burnham's managerial class won the twentieth century, and Fortune 500 executives are typically professional managers rather than domain experts or founders, but that model traded speed and adaptability for scalability and is now exhausting itself.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Supports a thesis that founder-led, agent-augmented firms can out-adapt professionally managed incumbents.
insights.quote: Most of the executives at Fortune 500 companies are not domain experts

insights.claim: Marc Andreessen suggests agents on top of a rigorous data foundation create a third model that preserves founder vitality while automating the coordination work that made the managerial layer necessary.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Argues for backing founder-led companies that scale with agents instead of hierarchy.

insights.claim: Elon Musk predicts companies with humans in the loop will lose, comparing it to a spreadsheet needing a person to calculate some cells, though the authors note forecasts for the fully autonomous company range from years to never.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: An extreme view; timelines are highly uncertain, so avoid pricing fully autonomous firms.
insights.quote: companies with “humans in the loop” will lose

insights.claim: The decline of managerialism will look like everyone becoming a manager: more people specifying work, delegating to agents, inspecting results and updating the process, ending the professional managerial class's monopoly on management rather than management itself.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Reframes AI labor impact as role change toward delegation and judgment, not just headcount cuts.
insights.locator: the irony is that the decline of managerialism

insights.claim: Software engineers' work is already shifting to scoping problems, delegating to parallel coding agents, and reviewing pull requests, a pattern expected to spread to other knowledge workers.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Leading indicator for how white-collar roles will restructure.
insights.locator: Software engineers are feeling this acutely today

insights.claim: Execution and judgment are economic complements, so as AI cheapens routine execution, demand for the judgment that directs it rises, which is good for human productivity and salaries.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Bullish for wages of high-judgment workers, bearish for procedure-following roles.
insights.locator: This is good news for human productivity and salaries

themes.theme: The sovereign firm and token capital

insights.claim: Because every competitor can rent the same frontier models, advantage comes from owning the learning loop: a bank that records facts, overrides, outcomes and policy adjustments keeps its edge when a better model arrives, while one that only records final decisions does not.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Moat shifts from model access to proprietary feedback data and evaluations; relevant to which enterprises capture AI value.

insights.claim: A sovereign firm can switch AI providers after a price rise, terms change or model retirement without losing what it has learned, an independence that grows more important as dependence on models grows.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Supports demand for portable, customer-owned data and model-agnostic infrastructure, a risk to lock-in strategies of model vendors.

insights.claim: Satya Nadella argues AI commoditizes human and organizational expertise, so companies must build both human capital and token capital, and that the learning loop between them becomes the firm's new IP.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: CEO of a key AI platform endorses owned AI capability as the new corporate asset.
insights.quote: this loop becomes the new IP of the firm

insights.claim: Jensen Huang said Nvidia, valued above $3 trillion with just 30,000 employees at the time, is one of the largest small companies in the world because of AIs built on data flywheels.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Revenue-per-employee extremes are the template investors may seek in AI-native firms.
insights.quote: one of the largest, small companies in the world

insights.claim: Data ownership alone is not a moat; the moat appears only when data and the AI reasoning over it improve decisions and products faster than competitors, though ownership prevents the firm's memory being trapped in a vendor's stack.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Warns against assuming that data hoards equal defensibility; look for demonstrated improvement loops.
insights.locator: Ownership alone is not a moat

themes.theme: Market outlook and the Databricks investment case

insights.claim: Falling coordination costs will let companies get more done with the people they have and enable new companies that never made sense before, because ten people will be able to do what used to take thousands.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Implies a wave of small-team companies and compression of headcount per revenue dollar.

insights.claim: A16z led Databricks' Series A in 2013 when it was seven Berkeley academics with only conference ticket revenue, and stepped in with NEA to lead a Series C nobody else would, two years before a roughly six-times-valuation acquisition offer that the company declined.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Illustrates a venture payoff from holding through a tempting sale; note the author is an interested investor.
insights.locator: The Best Idea You'll Ever Have

insights.claim: Horowitz argues the rarest combination is a huge market with an entrepreneur big enough to fulfill it, and that Databricks had both when it declined the offer.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Investor heuristic: weight founder-market ceiling fit over a near-term exit.
insights.quote: That’s the rarest of rare things.
insights.locator: The Best Idea You'll Ever Have
